messages.subject: Fragmented habitat mask construction
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I'm trying to estimate the density of brushtail possums within a small (<10ha) urban forest fragment. My study design consists of a single session over 8 nights with 70 live-capture cage traps.

Because my study is within a forest fragment surrounded by two other habitat types (grassy park and residential housing) that I do not expect homogenous density across, I'm in the process of creating a habitat mask (polygon shapefile) that separates the habitat into these three habitat types (see below: green for forest, orange for grassy park and pink for housing; traps are the dots). I've been following the density_surfaces pdf closely to do this. The shapefile contains a single field that classifies each polygon as 1,2 or 3 depending on their habitat type.

I have successfully loaded this shapefile into R as a spatial data frame, however when I try to use the make.mask function, I get this error message:

1: In make.mask(possumtrap, type = "trapbuffer", poly = jubilee_map) :
  some traps are not inside habitat polygon
2: In make.mask(possumtrap, type = "trapbuffer", poly = jubilee_map) :
  no points in mask

Which doesn't seem to make sense because as far as I can tell, my trap locations are all within the chosen polygons.

library(secr)

CH<-read.capthist("captfile.txt","trapfile.txt",detector="multi")
##creating the capthist object, assuming the multi detector is an okay approximation for my single-capture traps

library(rgdal)
datadir<-("~/Documents/Masters/THESIS YEAR 2019/secr/habitat mask")
jubilee_map <- rgdal::readOGR (dsn = datadir, layer = "jubilee_clipped_type")

possumtrap <- traps(CH[[1]])
##just extracting the coordinates of the traps from the CH possum capthist object

possummask <- make.mask(possumtrap, buffer = 280, type = "trapbuffer",
                        poly = jubilee_map, keep.poly = FALSE,check.poly = TRUE)

possummask <- addCovariates(possummask, jubilee_map)

Any help would be very much appreciated.

Let me know if you'd like more information.

Cheers,

Charlotte

messages.body_plain:
It would appear that the projections aren’t lining up perhaps? Although they look fine in your attached map.

You should also probably filter your polygons to remove the non-habitat, as you expect no home range centres there and didn’t sample that habitat. And then create a single poly for your habitat.

For example, if your poly is an sf object:

Habitat <- poly%>%filter(habitat%in%c(1:2))%>%summarise(mean=mean(habitat))

 make.mask (traps(CH), buffer = 30000, type = 'trapbuffer', spacing = 2000,
                        poly = as(Habitat, “Spatial”), poly.habitat = T, keep.poly = FALSE)

But that’s an issue for when you are sure the Habitat and traps are truly aligned in the right projection..

CL

messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I have a technical question related to equations 4/5 and the text between within Efford and Hunter 2018 in Biometrics. If I am understanding the text correctly,
ignoring the timing of marking; T is assumed ~ Poisson(mu), where mu is a product of e(density) and e(detections)|s_i integrated over the entire area but is likely to be overdispersed spatially because the actual location of si is not uniform. eq. 5 and thereabouts describes the penalty for Likelihood(T) and procedures for estimating c-hat. I guess I my question relates to some of the overdispersion calculations going on under the hood when the encounter model is binary and when there might be covariates involved (If I have not already demonstrated how poorly I understand this, the question will).  makes sense for a Poisson encounter model when lambda(s) is assumed to be homogeneous and the detection model is null.  It seems like the Bernoulli equivalent, where, say, p = 1-exp(-mu)), must involve summing the detections across K periods at the j detectors, where e(binomialcount_j)|parameters = p-hat_j*K? Maybe if lambda(s) is still assumed to be homogeneous and there are no detection covariates, extra variability in the j counts could be calculated relative to expectedVar(binomialcount_j)|parameters =  e(binomialcount_j)*(K- e(binomialcount_j))/K, or am I thinking about this incorrectly?  Particularly, I'm having trouble wrapping my head around what might be going on when e(binomialcount_j) varies across j. If have missed a description of this within the paper, I apologize--any insight is appreciated.

Thanks,

John

par(mfrow=c(3,3))

messages.subject: subset.capthist
messages.body_plain:
Hello secr masters,

I am working on roe deer density estimation. The sampling design was 29 camera-traps/km2 during 153 days of sampling. I would like to sub-sample the data to know how density results change with reduced number of cameras and reduced number of days. This will allow me to optimise the sampling effort for future studies and also to assess the appropriate sampling effort to identify a big proportion of the standing male roe deer population.

In my opinion, the best option would be to use the function subset.capthist(), subsetting for decreasing occasions and traps. Ideally, using a bootstrap approach with 100 iterations and plot the density results for the camera-subsampling and temporal-subsampling. Do you think that this make sense? Do you have other suggestions?

Thank you very much for your attention.

Best regards,

Amael Hinojo.

messages.body_plain:
You could do that. I wouldn't take the results too seriously as an indication of what might happen next time you sample, so 100 bootstraps might be over the top - maybe 1 would be enough to give you the picture.

You could also plug your parameter estimates into secrdesignapp (https://www.stats.otago.ac.nz/secrdesignapp/). That scrolls to a maximum of 100 occasions in the current version, but you can type in 153 or whatever. Subsetting detector locations is a bit trickier in secrdesignapp, but you can generate random or regular configurations in a region.

Murray

messages.subject_clean: estimating overdispersion in T matrix in SMR with bernoulli encounter model
messages.body_plain:
Hi John

Sorry for the delay. I suspect you're just overthinking this. We start by naively fitting a Poisson model, knowing that this will underestimate the variance. To bring the variance up to something reasonable we recompute with an empirical (simulation-based) estimate of the overdispersion c. Any complexity in the relationship between the detection model and c should be expressed in the simulations T_s. The relationship c-hat = var(T_s) / mean(T_s) just expresses the factor by which the simulation-based variance exceeds its Poisson expectation (= mean(T_s)).

So I'm arguing that the simulation-based adjustment does not require deeper understanding of the sort you seem to be chasing.

Murray

messages.subject: Habitat covariates
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I am trying to fit a large, multi-session (48) model with habitat covariates. For simplicity, I’ve constrained to two covariates here (secure habitat and food), both of which are expected to have positive relationships with density.

Fitting the following ’secr’ model:

secr.fit(capthist=ch, mask =mask2000b,
                    model = list(D~secure+food, lambda0~1, sigma ~1),
                    detectfn = 'HHN’, ncores = 4, method = "Nelder-Mead", start=sec)

I get this result:

A surprising negative relationship with food. To validate this finding, I predicted session-specific density estimates, averaged covariate values within each sessions mask, and did a simple linear model, where I should expect a similar result:

lm(d~secure+food, data=dens.table)

I get this result:

The expected, positive relationship with both covariates. There is a bit of a spatial scale difference here, the ’secr’ model is relating the density of home range centres to the covariate at the scale of the mask (4 sq. Km), while the linear model is at a larger scale of the session areas (500-2,000 sq. Km). But in general, if broad regions with more food have more bears, I would expect those individual bears to also locate their home ranges nearer to this food. It doesn’t seem likely that the bear density would be so strongly driven by food at a broad scale and then the animals avoid food at the their home range scale.

Has anyone experienced anything like this before or have any ideas on moving forward? Have a feeling reviewers would much rather see this in a clean ’secr’ model, as opposed to me pulling out the session-specific density estimates and doing a linear model. My sample size also drastically plummets with that approach too.

Cheers,
Clayton

messages.subject: Questions multi-session mark-resight models
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I am using the SECR package in order to estimate the density of wild dogs for a camera-trap study, with mark-resight multi-session models. The data spans over an entire year, divided into 4 sessions. The first 2 sessions correspond to the dry season and the last 2 sessions correspond to the wet season.

When running the multi-session models, I always need to specify autoini on session 2. Specifying autoini on any of the other sessions results in autoini failure and NA results for all estimates. So far, the multi-session models (using autoini on session 2) seem to work, although I sometimes get warning messages of the type ‘possible maximization error: nlm returned code 3’ or ‘possible maximization error: nlm returned code 4. See ?nlm’ or ‘probable maximization error: optim returned convergence 1’ or ‘at least one variance calculation failed’. I have ignored these error messages in some cases (or tried some tricks from the troubleshooting vignette in other cases), but these messages might be indicating more serious problems with my models. Some examples are provided below.

Here are the main issues that I have encountered with my models:

1. I obtain a value of pID = 1.0 for most of the models that I have ran so far. From my understanding, the argument details = list(knownmarks = FALSE) is necessary in my model since we do not know the number of marked animals in the population (we are using natural marks to identify individuals). When I remove the argument details = list(knownmarks = FALSE) from secr.fit, the pID becomes <1.0 but g0 then becomes equal to 1.0. Is this a normal behavior and if not, what does this indicate?

Hello Vanessa
I'm just going to pick off the questions I can easily answer right off.

1. These are model fitting issues for which it is hard to provide a confident answer. In general, if autoini is giving trouble then just specify starting values in the 'start' argument. nlm return code 3 is often OK, code 4 less so (exceeded max iterations). If you're worried about either you can check by re-starting the maximization using start = nameofpreviousfit. If the issue is just in the variance estimates (SE) then set method = 'none' at this point.

2. Yes, I think it's OK. The predict method with all.levels = TRUE is just providing more than you need.

3. I haven't looked at this

4. This is normal. I think the variation should/might disappear if you specified start rather than relying on autoini which has a stochastic component.

5. This would seem to be an iteraction between (4) and (1) - I haven't looked closely. Manually setting start values is probably the way to go.

6. 'secr' doesn't do this (note lower case). I included a function classMembership in openCR that does this for the different set of models in that package. The procedure is to estimate the likelihood components for each animal given membership in each class and assign a proportional probability of membership. Although in principle it could be implemented in 'secr' the coding is very different so it won't happen soon. On the other hand, you should not expect that the classes align with biological groups - they needn't 'represent' anything other than variability in the parameter. One might address your hypothesis of spatial variation in sigma via non-euclidean distance models, but I'm not going to push that as I foresee other complications and the signs are you have limited data..

Mark-resight methods seem fragile and I haven't used them much - I'm sorry I can't help more.

Murray

messages.body_plain:
Hi Stefano
What is this "a"? If you successfully model between-session movement in openCR.fit then the reported estimates of phi are estimates of actual survival. That is a big 'if': it depends on a good match between the study design and dispersal biology of your species, and on correct use of somewhat tricky software. You should at least use the latest version of openCR (1.4.1) that was only submitted yesterday to CRAN and is not yet fully distributed (but see section on movement kernels in  https://www.otago.ac.nz/density/pdfs/openCR-vignette.pdf).
Murray
